items.rss_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_description: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline Talent Gap ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:05 As AI automates entry-level insurance tasks, insurance industry leaders must design experiences to develop professional judgment in emerging talent. November 19, 2026 Image Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? That replacement system needs a name and, more importantly, an owner. Architecting Experience is the framework of deliberately designed exposures, decisions, and feedback loops through which people develop professional judgment and decision context. Cracks in the career ladder Stanford's Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll data on millions of U.S. jobs through June 2026 and found no economy-wide displacement from AI. What they did find was new employment among 22- to 25-year-olds lagging in industries heavily affected by AI, by about 19% compared to less-affected industries.[1] The employment ladder isn't broken, but some rungs at the bottom are disappearing, which makes it a whole lot harder to climb. Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. In their 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, PwC looked at over a billion job advertisements. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. Clear the slop from the stream BCG recently surveyed 11,749 workers across 14 markets about their use of AI at work. Two-thirds of regular AI users reported increased job satisfaction. At the same time, 41% reported increased mental strain. Half said they were spending more time managing and directing AI than doing the underlying work itself.[3] "Brain fry" refers to the mental fatigue associated with information overload from increased AI oversight.[4] With AI, any junior underwriter can generate a 40-page report with the aplomb of a managing director. But then, the report has to be checked. Preferably by someone with enough know-how to identify and correct mistakes. Without guardrails, we quickly end up in a system where our young talent can access AI-powered tools that allow them to produce work that looks good, but is actually riddled with problems. These problems are then sent upstream to more senior resources who have to spend their time fixing this "workslop"[5]. Junior professionals learn nothing in the process, and increase the workload of their most knowledgeable, and often most expensive, colleagues. When we claim AI is changing the way we work, we're giving the tool too much credit, while absolving ourselves of responsibility. The truth is, AI isn't changing the way we work. Our decision-makers are. And if, as a result of these changes and the adoption of AI, the leaders break the career ladder, they are responsible for engineering a new one. AI-resilient architecture I'm not in favor of clinging to rote work out of nostalgia. AI very much has a place in our workflows, and I remain bullish on the beneficial role of AI over the long term. But today, as we are all still sorting out the impacts and influences of AI on real people, we must think things through holistically and humanistically from the very beginning. In the face of AI removing traditional and lower-level tasks, the implications of this must be assessed, and solutions for the resultant gaps must be created. When architecting experience for new talent, what matters is to look at tasks through the dual lens of raw efficiency and professional development. Do the tasks teach the rules of the game, and more importantly, when the rules stop applying? Do they offer a chance to shadow a more seasoned professional to develop situational awareness and understanding of context? Do they help build judgment? Do they create the kinds of relationships every business is built on? These answers will help inform which tasks to automate, and which need more thought. A "yes" doesn't mean the task cannot be handed off to automation; it means the developmental value has to be preserved, somehow. The oversight role for management is to understand and enforce the right order of operations: organic brain first, neural network second. As with all complex systems, architecting experience isn't a blueprint. It's a process bound to yield different results for different organizations. Once the initial assessment is complete, ideally under the supervision of an executive with accountability, the hard work of execution, review, and adaptation begins. The good news is: there's plenty of responsibility to go around. Executive management must identify the experiences that create expertise, design a plan for succession, and own how the business will look ten years down the road. Elsewhere, HR and development teams have a responsibility to engineer the learning experiences and coaching or apprenticeship infrastructure, while managers can iterate, suggest improvements, and raise the red flag when skills aren't being developed. Tech and risk teams also have a clear role to observe AI usage, monitor costs and defect rates, and flag when automated work misses the mark. Senior professionals must keep in mind that juniors need engagement, context, and good professional models to follow, while the juniors themselves must remember to think first and ask AI second. Insurance is still early in the AI adoption process, and fortunate to have a deep bench of experienced professionals around the world, alongside ambitious newcomers. But every day, AI offers new deployment opportunities for efficiency and optimization. The greatest organizations of tomorrow will not only be able to harness those opportunities, but will also succeed in architecting experience for the next generation of world-class talent. References 1. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen. Stanford Digital Economy Lab. "Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence." Revised Aug. 12, 2026. Source 2. PwC. "2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer." June 15, 2026. Source 3. Boston Consulting Group. "AI at Work: Strategy Matters More Than Tools." June 3, 2026. Source 4. Boston Consulting Group and UC Riverside research, reported in Harvard Business Review. "When Using AI Leads to 'Brain Fry.'" March 2026. Source 5. BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab. "Workslop: The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Busywork." Sept. 15, 2025. Source Bob Pick

items.title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.original_title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.rss_title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.rss_description: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit? Risk Management ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:02 Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? November 19, 2026 Image On Dec. 18, Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters, and millions of us will happily pay to watch Earth's mightiest heroes face a villain bent on bringing the world to its knees. It's a great escape, partly because we know the heroes always show up in time. Real life offers no such guarantee, and last week showed how close we already live to our own doomsday script. Consider how recently the world ran on paper. Not long ago, people received a printed paycheck every week. Many of us remember our parents planning lunch hours around getting to the bank, or racing there Saturday morning before the branch closed at noon. Bills were paid by paper check, mailed to the mortgage company, the electric company and the oil company. Insuring a car or a house meant calling an agent. Buying anything "from a computer" was pure Isaac Asimov. Today, the entirety of human knowledge fits in a device the size of a deck of cards that nearly everyone carries in their pocket. That has been liberating. But it has also left us almost completely dependent on invisible systems we assume will always be on and safe from disruption, whether the threat is a malfunction, a cyberattack or simple human error. The past week showed how quickly those systems can grind to a halt. On Nov. 12, a Microsoft outage took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot – the backbone of millions of businesses – across dozens of countries for more than half a day. The next afternoon, a communications failure forced the FAA to ground every departing U.S. flight for more than four hours, the longest nationwide shutdown since 9/11. Then on Nov. 16, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase's own hardware disrupted online banking, branch transactions and Zelle payments, spilling over to customers at other banks doing business with Chase. Chase said there was no evidence the outage was cyber-related, and that is exactly the point. If an internal glitch can rattle America's biggest commercial bank, imagine what a deliberate, coordinated attack on power grids, water systems and communications networks could do. Governments urge households to keep emergency supplies, including cash, on hand. Is your company following the same advice? Do business continuity plans cover this? For many companies, the honest answer is "not really." Most plans are built for hurricanes, fires, the loss of a building and other localized events. Backups reside in another state, employees work from home, and operations shift to a recovery site. All of this assumes the Internet, the power grid, and the rest of the economy are still working somewhere . Financial regulators have pushed for more. In 2019, the FFIEC reframed its guidance from business continuity planning to business continuity management, with a focus on operational resilience and the ripple effects of outages across the financial system. The industry also created Sheltered Harbor , a standard for backing up critical customer account data nightly to an offline, air-gapped vault so customers can still reach their funds after a worst-case cyber event. Sheltered Harbor is now winding down, with its specification moving to its parent, FS-ISAC, but the principle stands. Still, even these measures assume someone, somewhere, can restore the data and run the systems. A nationwide, prolonged outage is a scenario few plans address head-on. Can companies function when the rest of the world can't? Not entirely. If customers can't reach essential services, payment rails are down and vendors go dark, no amount of preparation will preserve business as usual. But "not entirely" is materially different from "not at all." The goal is keeping your promises: knowing who your customers are, what they own and what you owe them, and honoring the most critical obligations through manual processes until systems return. After last week, many risk managers are likely asking those questions for the first time. Insurers and brokers with clear answers ready will earn trust before the next outage arrives. In the end, a policy or a bank account is a promise, and trust is what customers are really buying. A company that goes silent in a crisis may never regain it. One that shows up, even with a pen, a paper form, and a phone tree, will be remembered for it. Is it really possible to be fully prepared? In the movies, doomsday is averted by heroes in capes. In real life, it will be survived thanks to the continuity planner with a binder of printed procedures, the claims veteran who remembers how to cut a paper check, and the IT lead who already knows which vendor to call. They are the real superheroes. Now is the time to give them what they need. Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? Diane Brassard James Ballot

items.title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.original_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_description: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:15 Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. November 19, 2026 Image Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. Our part is to give new producers something worth sharing, so a prospect's first impression is the producer and not just the company behind them. Prefer to listen? items.extracted_text: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start | Insurance Thought Leadership Skip to main content Agent & Broker Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. Lynn Lavender November 19, 2026 Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. Host it don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. Our part is to give new producers something worth sharing, so a prospect's first impression is the producer and not just the company behind them. Prefer to listen? Results will be shared anonymously. items.title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.original_title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.rss_title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.rss_description: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech PaulCarroll Mon, 11/16/2026 - 17:10 When I ran the editing operation for the Wall Street Journal's European edition in the '80s, the "lockup" at midnight (or so) was frequently so chaotic that I posited what I called Carroll's law. Building on Murphy's law – everything that can go wrong will go wrong – Carroll's law said Murphy was an optimist. I'm feeling déjà vu , given all the technology-related chaos of the past week, centered on Friday the 13th, when all U.S. air traffic was shut down for hours and Microsoft's Outlook was only intermittently operating after a full-on outage the day before, for what amounts to the email backbone for the world economy. As much as there are individual reasons for those outages and other recent ones, the problems point to a pattern. The transition we're going through to a completely wired, AI world is so fundamental that two things are true: 1) We need to be a lot more careful about work like the upgrades to the FAA system, and we can head off a lot of problems if we are. 2) There will still be chaos from time to time, including for the insurance industry, especially as we start to roll out AI agents. So buckle up. Let's have a look. I first started thinking a couple of weeks ago about writing about the risks that arise from connecting everything to everything through the Internet of Things. The impetus was a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems throughout Europe – including in France, the U.K., Italy, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Estonia – followed by similar attacks on commissaries at U.S. military installations. The hackers raised the temperature inside 900 freezer units across 17 countries to as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, causing millions of dollars of food to go bad overnight and be thrown out. France, which suffered two-thirds of the attacks on freezers, blamed Iran, and geopolitical tensions could well lead to such attacks. North Korea, Russia and China all have active military cyber units. It's also possible that teenagers who in the past might have spraypainted graffiti on a school wall will now use AI to indulge their anger and show off in much more destructive ways. In any case, the cyber attacks show that the power of the IoT comes with a potential downside. Connecting essentially every device to every other device gives hackers more routes into systems they want to attack. And industrial systems, such as those that let supermarkets monitor and manage refrigeration centrally typically aren't built to the same security specifications that the main IT systems are. Insurers will have to be alert both about clients and about themselves. Clients may suffer theft, business interruption, claims of negligence against directors and officers, and so on. Insurers may face attacks themselves as they link to more sensors, third-party data sources, and providers of digital services such as payments. Insurers certainly make juicy targets, given all the important information they have on individuals and businesses. The Wall Street Journal published a story with the headline, " Supermarket-Fridge Hacks Show Risk of Linking Everything to the Internet" , that said: "Artificial intelligence suddenly makes the problem much bigger, because hackers are automating their hunt for exposed web connections and running searches at blistering speeds." The article adds that 20% of IoT devices already have at least one known cybersecurity vulnerability. It turns out, though, that the refrigerator cyberattacks were just the start. On Thursday, bleeding into Friday, Microsoft's Outlook email system went down. As Wired wrote in a story headlined " The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World ": " The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge." Full details on the cause of the outage have yet to be provided. At the least, it shows the danger of concentration for a key service such as communication. We've actually seen even more, though smaller, examples of dangerous concentration just since Friday. United Airlines, which controls a major chunk of air travel in the U.S. and internationally, had to delay all departing flights for more than an hour and a half on Monday because of a software issue. A technical glitch with software at Chase Bank delayed online banking and caused transaction glitches for both itself and other major banks. Concentration will only increase from here, so we need to be prepared for the fact that a single problem can cause widespread trouble. There is some speculation that AI may have played a role in the Outlook trouble, given that Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees in July and just offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 people, or 27% of its workforce, while saying the company is turning more coding work over to AI. Which brings us to the FAA communications disaster that shut down air travel for five hours in the U.S. on Friday. The current official explanation is that a single, old router in Arkansas was overwhelmed during an upgrade to new technology, but some officials initially said an upgrade to AI technology known as SMART may also have been involved. Oddly, the disagreement is very public and at the cabinet level – the secretary of Transportation insists the AI work had no bearing on the outage, while the secretary of Homeland Security has suggested at least twice that the AI initiative may have been to blame. Whatever the exact problem, the FAA issue should be the simplest to avoid. It just requires some basic hygiene. For instance, you have to give yourself a way to instantly undo an upgrade if it starts to go south. And whatever you do, you don't do a major upgrade during a busy period -- such as a Friday afternoon, when millions of people are flying somewhere for the weekend. You do the upgrade in the middle of the night, when a problem can be corrected before much of anyone notices. But people will ignore basic principles of software management, just as they'll be too reliant on single sources of key digital services such as communication and will be too slow to tackle the vulnerabilities that come from connecting to systems and services that aren't secure enough. And AI will greatly accelerate the pace at which problems surface. So we should consider recent events as warnings of future problems, not as one-offs. There is good news in the short term, though, for those of you who are superstitious types. Friday wasn't just the 13th; an astrology-curious acquaintance tells me Mercury and Venus both ended their retrogrades that day, bringing some supposed relief after weeks of celestial troublemaking. (Mercury, I'm told, can be especially problematic. It's blamed for everything from miscommunications to travel mishaps.) items.title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.original_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_description: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

items.extracted_text: Minnesota Workplace Injury and Illness Rate Reaches Record Low Article 0 Comments Minnesota’s estimated workplace injury and illness rate decreased from 2024 to 2025 and remains at its lowest rate since the measurement started in 1973, according to annual survey of occupational injuries and illnesses. Minnesota state had an estimated 2.8 OSHA-recordable nonfatal workplace injuries and illnesses per 100 full-time-equivalent (FTE) workers in 2025 the estimated rate for 2024 was 2.9 cases per 100 FTE workers. The survey estimated Minnesota had 64,800 workers with OSHA-recordable nonfatal workplace injuries and illnesses in 2025, compared to 66,000 estimated cases for 2024. Injuries accounted for 62,100 (96%) total recordable cases in 2025 illnesses were an additional 2,700 cases. In 2024, there were 3,400 illnesses. In 2025, Minnesota’s employment covered by the survey was approximately 2.92 million workers, compared to 2.89 million workers in 2024. items.extracted_text: AI-fueled Cyberattacks Drive Claims Surge at Japan Insurers Article 0 Comments Japan’s biggest property insurers are reporting a sharp jump in cyber insurance claims as artificial intelligence-driven attacks grow more sophisticated and hacking incidents surge nationwide. Tokio Marine Holdings Inc. received three times as many cyber insurance claim notifications in October as usual, according to the company. Sompo Holdings Inc. said claims in October were running at 2.5 times higher than the average over the one-year period ending Sept. 30, 2026. Both insurers disclosed the figures at earnings briefings on Thursday. Related: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard Say Third-Party Vendors Targeted in Cyberattack Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorized access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan. The increase in claims raises the risk of costly payouts even as rising numbers of incidents fuel demand for protection. Payouts on cyber policies could rise, but the surge has yet to translate into a significant earnings hit. Yoshinari Endo, a managing executive officer at Tokio Marine, said his company expects some impact on full-year results, though it is managing the profit risk and expects losses to stay within the assumptions of its initial annual plan. Junsuke Koike, an executive vice president at Sompo, said inquiries about raising coverage amounts or adding coverage items had tripled from normal levels. Japan’s experience mirrors a broader rise in cyber claims globally. US insurers reported more than 56,000 cyber claims in 2025, up 20% from a year earlier, while large companies are facing increasingly costly incidents. Cyber policies typically cover damages owed for data breaches, recovery costs and profits lost from disruptions, making insurance a growing part of corporate risk management. Cyber insurance penetration in Japan remains low for smaller companies. A 2025 survey by the General Insurance Association of Japan found that only 8.8% of small and medium-sized business owners said they had cyber insurance as a defense against attacks. Yasuko Fukuda, a senior executive officer at MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings Inc., said at an earnings briefing on Thursday that there is “significant room for the market to expand.” The insurers are trying to limit losses by helping customers prevent attacks. Starting in December, Sompo will offer a new service with Trend Micro Inc. and others that monitors for vulnerabilities on the internet. Insurers are being selective about underwriting. Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten coverage terms depending on a customer’s risk profile, Endo said. The company expects its cyber insurance business to remain profitable in the fiscal year through March 2027. Standard total payout limits in Japan and overseas run from about ¥100 million (about $630,000) to several hundred million yen per contract. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Allied World lowers pricing again for still $375m 2001 CAT Re 2026-1 catastrophe bond - Artemis.bm Allied World lowers pricing again for still $375m 2001 CAT Re 2026-1 catastrophe bond 20th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Allied World Assurance Company’s (AWAC) latest catastrophe bond sponsorship remains at the upsized $375 million target, but pricing has been lowered again for the three tranches of notes on offer, as the company is seeking strong execution with its 2001 CAT Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) deal, Artemis can report. Global insurance and reinsurance firm Allied World Assurance Company, part of the Fairfax Financial group, made its return to the catastrophe bond market for a renewal and expansion of its protection earlier this month. As we’ve explained before, Allied World’s $275 million 2001 CAT Re 2023-1 cat bond is set to mature at the end of this year, which effectively makes this new 2026-1 issuance a renewal and expansion of sorts. AWAC was initially targeting a $325 million source of annual aggregate retrocessional reinsurance protection from this 2001 CAT Re Series 2026-1 catastrophe bond deal. However, as we reported in our first update on this transaction, Allied World looked to obtain even more multi-peril retrocessional reinsurance protection than originally sought from this deal, as the target size was raised to $375 million. We also learned that the price guidance for each of the tranches of notes on offer had been lowered, with all three notes receiving new ranges offered below their initial guidance. We’re now told that the upsized $375 million target remains, but Allied World is still aiming to secure that protection at a more cost-effective rate, as the price guidance has been lowered once again for each of the three tranches of notes on offer. As we’ve previously said, at a $375 million size, Artemis’ data shows that this new cat bond for AWAC is targeted to become the company’s largest catastrophe bond sponsorship so far. View details of every catastrophe bond sponsored by Allied World in the Artemis Deal Directory . So, 2001 CAT Re Ltd. continues to offer catastrophe bond investors three tranches of Series 2026-1 notes, that are targeted to secure $375 million of retrocessional limit to protect Allied World and subsidiaries against losses from U.S named storms, U.S. and Canada earthquakes, and European windstorm risks. The protection from these notes will run on an annual aggregate and industry-loss trigger basis across three annual risk periods from January 1st 2027. The Class A tranche of notes remain at their $225 million size. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 5.4% and were first marketed to cat bond investors with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 9% and 9.5%, which was first lowered to a revised range of 8.25% and 9%, and we’re now told have been lowered to a revised range of 7.75% and 8.25%. What was a $50 million Class B tranche of notes were later upsized to $75 million, which is where they remain in size. These Class B notes come with an initial base expected loss of 8.7% and were first offered to investors with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 14% and 15%, which was first lowered to a revised range of 13.25% to 14%, and have now been lowered again to a revised range of 12.75% and 13.25%. And lastly, what was initially a $50 million Class C tranche of notes were also later upsized to $75 million, which is where they remain in size, we are told. These Class C notes come with an initial base expected loss of 11.69% and were first marketed with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 19% and 20%, which was later lowered to a revised range of 18.25% to 19%, and have now been lowered once again to a revised spread of 17.75% and 18.25%. This looks set to be a great result for Allied World, as the company is set to secure its largest catastrophe bond sponsorship so far, and with the pricing for all three tranches of notes lowering once again, this shows that the company is capitalising on market conditions to lock-in well-priced aggregate protection. As a reminder, you can read all about this new 2001 CAT Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) catastrophe bond and view details of more than 1,250 other cat bond transactions in the Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: NC Farm Bureau sponsoring its third catastrophe bond, $475m Blue Ridge Re 2026-1 - Artemis.bm NC Farm Bureau sponsoring its third catastrophe bond, $475m Blue Ridge Re 2026-1 20th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The North Carolina Farm Bureau is back and looking to sponsor its third catastrophe bond, this time targeting a $475 million issuance of Blue Ridge Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) cat bond notes to further built-out capital markets backed multi-peril reinsurance, Artemis has learned. The North Carolina Farm Bureau is a non-profit general farm organisation that also provides financial services to its members, including insurance products. The North Carolina Farm Bureau (NC Farm Bureau) secured $400 million of indemnity and per-occurrence named storm reinsurance with its debut Blue Ridge Re 2023-1 cat bond issuance in late 2023. The insurer returned a year ago and secured $500 million of reinsurance from its second cat bond Blue Ridge Re 2025-1 , which gave it both per-occurrence and its first annual aggregate protection across a wider range of perils. For its third catastrophe bond, we understand that the NC Farm Bureau is seeking just per-occurrence protection again, but for the wider range of perils that featured in the 2025-1 issuance. The $400 million Blue Ridge Re 2023-1 cat bond’s coverage matures at the end of this year, so this Series 2026-1 issuance looks set to be a renewal and potential expansion of that protection, given it already has a larger potential target size from the start. NC Farm Bureau is again using its Bermuda based special purpose insurer (SPI) named Blue Ridge Re Ltd. for its latest catastrophe bond sponsorship. There are five tranches of notes on offer under this Series 2026-1 issuance, which together currently total $475 million. It’s worth noting though that this is one of those cat bonds with tranches that match in every way except the terms of coverage, so there is always a chance a sponsor opts to only place some of them dependent on investor demand. So, Blue Ridge Re Ltd. is offering five tranches of Series 2026-1 catastrophe bond notes to investors, with each set to provide reinsurance covering losses in the state of North Carolina to its main underwriting entities, which are usually the North Carolina Farm Bureau Insurance Company and Farm Bureau Insurance of North Carolina. Global reinsurance giant Hannover Re will again assist as the ceding reinsurer, we understand, entering into a retrocession agreement with the issuer Blue Ridge Re and then passing on the reinsurance protection to the NC Farm Bureau insurers. The notes will provide NC Farm Bureau with up to four years of coverage, across the next calendar years, with two tranches targeting three year protection and three tranches targeting four years. All five tranches of notes will provide NC Farm Bureau with reinsurance on a per-occurrence and indemnity trigger basis, covering losses from North Carolina named storm, severe thunderstorm and winter storm events, we are told. A $100 million Class A1 tranche of notes will have a three year term and would attach their coverage at $1 billion of losses and exhaust it at $1.65 billion, giving them an initial attachment probability of 1.62%, an initial base expected loss of 1.16% and they are being offered to investors with price guidance for a spread of between 2.75% and 3%. An also $100 million Class A2 tranche of notes will have a four year term and cover the same layer, so have identical risk metrics and initial price guidance. A $100 million Class B1 tranche of notes will have a three year term and are riskier, attaching their coverage at $500 million of losses and exhausting it at $1 billion, giving them an initial attachment probability of 3.7%, an initial base expected loss of 2.41% and they are being offered to investors with price guidance for a spread of between 5% and 5.5%. An also $100 million Class B2 tranche of notes will have a four year term and cover the same layer, so have identical risk metrics and initial price guidance. The final $75 million Class C1 tranche of notes will have a four term and are riskier still, attaching their coverage at $300 million of losses and exhausting it at $500 million, giving them an initial attachment probability of 6.58%, an initial base expected loss of 4.92% and they are being offered to investors with price guidance for a spread of between 8% and 8.5%. It’s good to see the NC Farm Bureau returning again and looking to further expand the reinsurance protection it receives from the catastrophe bond market this year. It will be interesting to see if all five tranches are placed and also whether they upsize, as this issuance could have the potential to grow meaningfully if investor demand is sufficient. items.extracted_text: Liberty Mutual targets $300m multi-peril reinsurance with twelfth Mystic Re cat bond - Artemis.bm Liberty Mutual targets $300m multi-peril reinsurance with twelfth Mystic Re cat bond 20th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Liberty Mutual Insurance has returned to the catastrophe bond market with an initial target to secure $300 million of indemnity based, multi-peril catastrophe reinsurance protection from the capital markets through a Mystic Re IV Ltd. (Series 2027-1) offering, Artemis can report. Notably, this is now the fifth year in a row that Liberty Mutual Insurance has returned to the catastrophe bond market late in the year to sponsor a new multi-year arrangement. These annual offerings are now helping the company layer capital markets backed catastrophe protection within its reinsurance tower, while staggering the multi-year coverages maturities at the same time. This is also the twelfth cat bond sponsorship by the insurer, all of which have taken the name Mystic Re, the first having been in June 2006. View details of every catastrophe bond sponsored by Liberty Mutual in our Deal Directory , where you can filter the results by trigger type and other features. Liberty Mutual’s $300 million Mystic Re IV 2024-1 cat bond that provided industry-loss index triggered protection is scheduled to mature at the end of this year, so this new 2027-1 offering continues the trend for the insurer to revert to indemnity trigger coverage as it looks to renew capital markets protection. For this Series 2027-1 catastrophe bond offering, Liberty Mutual is again utilising its Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (SPI) Mystic Re IV Ltd., making this the seventh series under that vehicle. Two tranches of Series 2027-1 notes are being offered to cat bond investors, with the issuance designed to provide Liberty Mutual at least $300 million in multi-peril, multi-year collateralized reinsurance protection. The notes will provide reinsurance protection to Liberty Mutual and its affiliates, running across a three calendar year term, from January 1st 2027 to the end of 2029, sources explained. The Mystic Re IV 2027-1 cat bond notes will provide Liberty Mutual with reinsurance protection against losses from named storms, earthquakes, severe weather and wildfires on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis, with the covered area being the US, Canada and the Caribbean. This is the same as the previous two Mystic Re cat bond offerings. A currently $100 million tranche of Class A notes will attach their coverage at $2.625 billion of losses and exhausting at $2.85 billion, which gives them an initial attachment probability of 2.27%, an initial expected loss of 2.07%, and we’re told these notes are offered with spread price guidance in a range from 4% to 4.5%. A currently $200 million Class B tranche will attach lower down at $2.075 billion of losses and exhausting at $2.425 billion, which gives them an initial attachment probability of 3.73%, an initial expected loss of 3.19%, and we’re told these notes are offered with spread price guidance in a range from 5.5% to 6%. The price guidance of the two tranches of notes indicates comparably lower multiples than Liberty’s recent issuances, reflecting the tighter spread environment in the catastrophe bond market. The partnership officially became effective on August 31, 2026. items.extracted_text: SafePoint raises Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond target again to $225m - Artemis.bm SafePoint raises Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond target again to $225m 20th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard SafePoint Insurance Company has raised the target size for its Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-4) catastrophe bond sponsorship a second time, now seeking an upsized $225 million or more of reinsurance protection to add to its recently priced indemnity deal, this publication has learned. Earlier this month, SafePoint returned to the catastrophe bond market to effectively add a third layer to its recently secured $650 million indemnity and per-occurrence Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) cat bond, which features two tranches of notes, providing named storm reinsurance protection to both SafePoint and its reciprocal exchanges. Once priced and secured, this Nature Coast Re 2026-4 issuance will sit above the 2026-2 tranches, so extending the same protection higher up SafePoint’s reinsurance tower. Once finalised, this will also become SafePoint’s fourth successful catastrophe bond sponsorship this year. SafePoint was initially looking to secure another $100 million layer of reinsurance protection through this new Nature Coast Re Series 2026-4 offering. In our first update on this transaction, we learned that SafePoint was targeting a slight upsizing for the deal, increasing it to provide $125 million of reinsurance protection, while at the same time, the price guidance for the notes on offer had been revised to the mid-point of the initial guidance range. Sources tell us that the target size has been increased for a second time, with SafePoint now aiming to close this Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond at more than double the initial target size, with a $225 million issuance or more being targeted by the insurer. With these second updates in mind, Nature Coast Re is now targeting issuance of a single $225 million or more tranche of Series 2026-4 Class AAA catastrophe bond notes, that will provide fully-collateralized reinsurance protection to SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges that the company operates. The notes will cover losses from named storms across the states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, which is the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. As we’ve said in previous articles on this deal, the coverage tracks the same as well, being on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis. The fully-collateralized reinsurance protection will run across a four-year period from December 1st, which is also the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. The Series 2026-4 Class AAA notes come with an initial base expected loss of 0.46% and were initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 3% and 3.5%. As we reported, that price guidance narrowed to the mid-point of the initial range at 3.25%, which is where they still remain, according to our sources. Once again, SafePoint continues to demonstrate a growing appetite, taking advantage of market conditions in the catastrophe bond space to lock-in significantly more multi-year protection that will give the firm meaningful certainty on its reinsurance for the coming year. SafePoint has been one of the biggest cat bond sponsors of 2026 so far in limit terms. Back in February, the insurer priced its Nature Coast Re 2026-1 issuance, which provided the firm with $250 million of indemnity protection. This past month has been extremely busy for SafePoint. The insurer recently secured $750 million of total cat bond protection through its largest sponsorship to date, as the firm managed to secure its upsized $650 million Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) deal last week. Earlier this week, SafePoint secured its targeted $100 million source of annual aggregate and industry-loss index triggered named storm protection from the Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 issuance. If the firm manages to secure this Nature Coast Re 2026-4 deal at its $225 million upsizing, it will take total cat bond backed reinsurance limit secured in recent weeks to $975 million for SafePoint, and for the year in total to a staggering $1.225 billion. items.extracted_text: BREAKING: Florida Citizens’ CEO Cerio to Step Down in January Article 0 Comments He oversaw Citizens Property Insurance Corp. during one of the most turbulent periods for Florida’s insurance market, seeing the state-created insurer grow to record size—then shrink to its smallest level in more than 20 years. And now Citizens’ CEO Tim Cerio is stepping down. “After nearly four incredibly rewarding years as your president/CEO and executive director, I will be leaving Citizens in January to return to the private sector,” Cerio said in a message to Citizens staff on Friday, Nov. 20. Cerio, who took over in January 2023 after former CEO Barry Gilway retired, did not indicate what endeavors he may pursue. He is a lawyer who served as general counsel for Citizens in 2015 and 2016. It’s also unclear who may be considered to replace Cerio at Citizens. “Over the next several weeks I will be working with our Board of Governors on a transition plan, so stay tuned for more specifics,” Cerio’s message reads. Cerio Cerio, who earned his bachelor’s degree and his law degree from the University of Florida, took the reins near the worst of the Florida property insurance crisis, in which 10 insurance carriers went insolvent and rates had soared. That caused policyholders across the state to move to Citizens, where premium increases are limited by statute. By September 2023, Citizens’ policy count reached more than 1.4 million, making it the largest property insurer in the state, by far. After enactment of 2022 and 2023 legislative changes that stemmed runaway claims litigation, Citizens has shrunk to 216,447 policies in force as of the end of October this year. “The reforms enacted by the Florida Legislature provided the tools to change course,” Cerio noted in his text message. “But legislation alone doesn’t create results.” He said Citizens has become a more-focused organization while it has maintained financial discipline and readiness. He thanked staff members for their hard work and flexibility through the years. Shrinking an organization can be more challenging than growing one, he said. “Many of you took on new responsibilities, adapted to changing processes and supported colleagues through transitions,” he noted. Citizens Board Chairman Carlos Beruff praised Cerio’s leadership. “Mr. Cerio has been a steady, principled leader for Citizens during one of the most critical periods in the history of Florida’s property insurance market,” Beruff said in a statement sent by Citizens Friday morning. “Tim has a long track record of public service, and he leaves Citizens stronger and better positioned for the future. On behalf of the Board, I thank him for his service to Citizens and to the people of Florida.” Cerio will continue as a member of Governor-elect Byron Donalds’ transition team and as vice chairman of the Board of Governors of the State University System, the Citizens press release noted. items.extracted_text: California Probing If Nvidia Misled Investors on China Risks Article 0 Comments Nvidia Corp. is being investigated by California officials to determine whether any of its actions resulted in advanced chips or confidential information being improperly obtained by China. The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said in a statement Thursday that his office is also looking into whether the company misled investors about the situation. Nvidia was sent a subpoena seeking information to determine if the company violated the state’s corporate security law, he said. Related: Nvidia Scandal Raises New Concerns About Scale of Chinese Spying Jensen Huang’s disclosure last week of an extramarital affair plunged Nvidia into an unprecedented crisis, fueling a sharp selloff in the company’s shares and resulting in his ouster as chief executive officer. His disclosure also led to potential national security concerns following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang and that US officials suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Also on Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released confidential information showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year as of May, including to some that were later added to a Pentagon list of businesses accused of aiding China’s military. Nvidia’s logo Photographer: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.” Santa Clara, California-based Nvidia did not respond to a message seeking comment. Nvidia is the world’s largest chipmaker and was, until recently, the world’s most valuable publicly-traded company. Under Huang’s leadership its products became central to the massive build out in artificial intelligence infrastructure. In a Bloomberg Television interview on Tuesday, Bonta described the situation as “very possibly” something his office could examine. He added that his course of action would be determined by whether any California laws could have been broken, which would establish jurisdiction for his office. Beijing has denied that it attempted to spy on Jensen Huang, who is not related to Alice Huang. On Tuesday, Huang expressed a willingness to return to the helm although the board isn’t currently considering such an idea, Bloomberg News reported. Bonta, a Democrat who won reelection earlier this month, has been scrutinizing Big Tech more broadly, including by filing a lawsuit against OpenAI for allegedly violating the state’s unfair competition law by unsafely developing its AI products.
